messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I'm trying to publish a paper where I model the distribution of fish in a Stream Network using Detection-Occupation models.

As Goodness of Fitness tests I compute a Bayesian p-value and I've calculated a posterior distribution of AUC as proposed by Zipikin et al. 2012:
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/11-1936.1/abstract

However I have a reviewer proposing to evaluate the the model predicting ability against an independent data set. The reviewer advised to withhold a subset of the sites from the model construction and use it to evaluate the model performance.

Although this it's standard for other SDM methods (e. g.: Max Ent) I don't recall seen it in Detection-Occupation models. Does any one has some references of this?

Any help would be apreciated!

Cheers:
Mário

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mario,

Our group has done this sort of thing in a couple of papers:

McCarthy, K. P., R. J. Fletcher, Jr., C. T. Rota, and R. L. Hutto.  2012.  Predicting species distributions from samples collected along roadsides.  Conservation Biology 26:68-77.

Rota, C. T., R. J. Fletcher, Jr., J. M. Evans, and R. L. Hutto. 2011. Does accounting for imperfect detection improve species distribution models?  Ecography 34: 659-670.

It is a bit tricky regarding how to deal appropriately with imperfect detection on the validation data, however. We tried a couple of ways in Rota et al, but I would imagine there are better ways to do so. I would imagine there are other papers out there as well (I think I have seen a few, but I don’t recall the citations off hand).

Hope that is helpful.

All the best,

Rob

Hi Mario,

I recently used cross-validation for model selection for occupancy models, and found it to be a good way to compare model performances. Although the paper describes the technique for multi-species models, it should be straightforward to apply the same methods to the single-species models.  (Cross-validation involves splitting the data into k subsets, withholding one at a time, and calculating a model performance statistic on each hold-out data set.)

Broms, K.M., M.B. Hooten, and R.M. Fitzpatrick. In press. Model selection and assessment for multi-species occupancy models.  Ecology.  DOI: 10.1890/15-1471.1

Cheers,
Kristin

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mario,

I will let the Bayesian experts on the group answer your question, but I would say that the decision on holding out data depends a bit on the ultimate goal. If the goal is to understand how well a model predicts to unsampled locations, k-fold validation is useful, but prospective sampling (independent sampling of new locations or times) is better because the data are more independent than the data used for model building, leading to a more realistic assessment of the model to predict well in space or time. Also, in the SDM literature there has been some criticism of simple k-fold validation because it can result in folds that are not independent samples, leading to the selection of overly complex models (see Wegner and Olden 2012, Methods Ecol Evol, as an example). As a potential solution, some have advocated ‘block’ validation in regards to leaving data out, where entire geographic blocks are removed rather than a random sample points in the k-fold partition.

All the best,

Rob

messages.body_plain:
HI Mario,

The MCMC iterations provide an estimation of the posterior distributions given the data.  If each iteration were run on a different portion of the data, then you would no longer have the same interpretation of the chains.

The purpose of the k-fold validation is to mimic the more ideal setting of having an independent/ hold-out data set to test the models. If different data were selected for each iteration, it would no longer mimic the hold-out data set.  In machine learning, they often split their data into training (to build the models) and testing (to compare model performance). However, in ecology the data sets are usually smaller and there is not enough data to be comfortable completely withholding a large portion of the data when building the models.

The k-fold validation does require one to run the model k times, but with today's parallel processing and cloud servers, this is not as burdensome as it once was. I've been lucky to have department servers on which I run my models but a colleague of mine found Amazon's cluster computing to be invaluable for his dissertation (https://aws.amazon.com/hpc/). Also, you use the same exact BUGS/ JAGS code that has already been created when building the model. I find that I have to run the model so many times in my model building and testing, that the CV ends up not being as burdensome as the model building.

~Kristin

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mario,

The trouble with measuring predictive ability in species distribution models is that most or all typically used statistics (e.g., AUC) are no longer appropriate once you formally recognize measurement error, as does an occupancy model. Testing how well a model predicts the (error-prone) observations is not a very interesting way of measuring prediction success in my view. What you would like to do is measure how well the model is able to predict the true presence/absence state.

In this respect, perhaps the best test of predictive ability for occupancy models that I have seen was in a paper by Petr Keil (around 2013 or 2014): they used ebird data for highly surveyed quadrats to validate a model applied to some atlas data set. For the ebird data, they chose quadrats that were more than 20 times visited within a year, so for all reasonable values of detection probability they could assume that the presence/absence status was ascertained without error (note: the combined detection probability over 20 independent visits is >0.98 for a species with per-visit p of 0.2). Then, they had a data set with assumed known truth and could evaluate the predictive success of their model against it.

Best regards  --- Marc

I recently used cross-validation for model selection for occupancy models, and found it to be a good way to compare model performances. Although the paper describes the technique for multi-species models, it should be straightforward to apply the same methods to the single-species models.  (Cross-validation involves splitting the data into k subsets, withholding one at a time, and calculating a model performance statistic on each hold-out data set.)

Broms, K.M., M.B. Hooten, and R.M. Fitzpatrick. In press. Model selection and assessment for multi-species occupancy models.  Ecology.  DOI: 10.1890/15-1471.1

Dear Mario,

I don’t think that your approach is wrong. It looks straightforward: you compare an observed response with what they model says this response should be. This has been done, I believe, for occupancy models by Rota et al. (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2010.06433.x/abstract).

However, I just think that such a test is perhaps not very relevant when you have nondetection measurement error in your response and when your model formally acknowledges this, as is a hallmark of occ models. In this case, you would rather want to gauge the goodness of a model by how well it predicts the true presence/absence. This distinction has been made in the recent paper by Jose Lahoz Monfort (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/geb.12138/abstract):

Because the aim of SDMs is to

model species distributions, it is critical to assess their performance

in executing exactly this task, and not according to

another criterion such as in Rota et al. (2011) and Comte &

Grenouillet (2013). Assessing how well a given method can

predict detections is not the same as assessing how well a model

can describe or predict the spatial distribution of occupied sites.

So if you can get a detection-free data set then I would prefer to measure the goodness of your model by comparing its predictions of presence-absence with the known truth in this data set, which I find a wonderful idea that I first read in a paper by Petr Keil (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ddi.12199/full).

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Mario,

The trouble with measuring predictive ability in species distribution models is that most or all typically used statistics (e.g., AUC) are no longer appropriate once you formally recognize measurement error, as does an occupancy model. Testing how well a model predicts the (error-prone) observations is not a very interesting way of measuring prediction success in my view. What you would like to do is measure how well the model is able to predict the true presence/absence state.

In this respect, perhaps the best test of predictive ability for occupancy models that I have seen was in a paper by Petr Keil (around 2013 or 2014): they used ebird data for highly surveyed quadrats to validate a model applied to some atlas data set. For the ebird data, they chose quadrats that were more than 20 times visited within a year, so for all reasonable values of detection probability they could assume that the presence/absence status was ascertained without error (note: the combined detection probability over 20 independent visits is >0.98 for a species with per-visit p of 0.2). Then, they had a data set with assumed known truth and could evaluate the predictive success of their model against it.

Best regards  --- Marc

Although the paper describes the technique for multi-species models, it should be straightforward to apply the same methods to the single-species models.  (Cross-validation involves splitting the data into k subsets, withholding one at a time, and calculating a model performance statistic on each hold-out data set.)

Broms, K.M., M.B. Hooten, and R.M. Fitzpatrick. In press. Model selection and assessment for multi-species occupancy models.  Ecology.  DOI: 10.1890/15-1471.1

Cheers,

NIMBLE doesn’t directly support logical indexing or which().  But it does allow one to provide a new function for use in BUGS code.  Writing a function to find the indices of true values of a logical operation would be possible, but another issue would be that BUGS code normally requires fixed-size objects.  The size of the return value of which() in R depends on the arguments, so it’s not a very natural fit to BUGS.  Can you provide more context of how you want to use the results of the which() statement?  It might be possible to write a function that includes the which() as a step internally towards whatever it is you need.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

AR is the sum of recruitable individuals (i.e., individuals in the augmented set that have never been alive). You could do something like this:

for(t in 2:T) {
  ER[t] <- exp(gamma0 + gamma1*x1[t] + ...) # Could include DD or make it per-capita
  AR[t] <- sum(recruitable[,t-1])
  b[t] <- ER[t] / AR[t] # Entrance probs
  }

for(i in 1:M) {
  for(t in 1:T) {
    recruitable[i,t] <- 1-max(z[i,1:t])
    }
   }

Note that ER must be less than AR, but as long as this condition is met with the initial values, it will hold. So initialize gamma0 to -20 or something.

Richard

Dear Tyler,

thanks for your email. Please see below for some comments, interspersed in blue. I also copy to the HMecology list, because I find your email of general interest.

Best regards  --  Marc

From: Hallman, Tyler [Tyler....@oregonstate.edu]
Sent: 22 April 2016 22:53
To: Kery Marc
Subject: Questions on predicting abundance

Hi Marc,

I attended a workshop from you and Andy at Patuxent a couple years ago. At the time this type of hierarchical statistics was completely new to me. I've been teaching myself ever since. I bought your book (Applied Hierachical Modeling in Ecology)  MK: excellent ! ;)  , and have gone through most of the pertinent sections. I'm at the point of analyzing data for my dissertation, and I am planning on using the Time-Removal/DS model for my avian point count data. It seems like running this type of model is easier in the Bayesian framework than ML at least in part because you've shown how to do it. I don't recall seeing any way to do this type of model with unmarked in the book. Is no such function readily available in unmarked? MK: No such function in unmarked.

I have one other big question, and perhaps I'm just missing this somewhere. When using unmarked, the function predict can be quite useful to predict abundance on a landscape based on a model created with unmarked. Is there a good way to make similar landscape level predictions with Bayesian models? I don't recall any examples of this in the book.
MK: That's a quite good point actually ! I am afraid there is no direct example of this, except  for the example for species richness  on page 713.

Basically, you can of course do such predictions fairly easily in BUGS software and you can do this in one of two ways:
(1) the simplest is to provide the covariate values for all pixels in your real landscape as data for BUGS and then add a line in the code that computes the expected abundance for those sites, using (a) the parameter values estimated in the model and (b) the landscape values of the covariates provided in the data bundle. If your landscape is not too large (e.g., has less than a couple of thousands pixels), then I would probably do that. Here, of course, you will automatically get the whole posterior distribution of the predictions, so you can easily plot the predictions (meaning, their posterior mean) as well as the posterior standard deviation or the lower and upper bound of the 95% credible interval.
(2) Especially if you have a large domain (MANY pixels), it is easier to do these predictions outside of BUGS, in R, as we do in the species richness example in the book mentioned above. Then, you take the parameter estimates from BUGS and "combine" them with the values of the covariates in your landscape to obtain the predicted abundance. In this approach it is perhaps easier to get the posterior mean only, but it is safer to obtain the full posterior of the predictions and then get the posterior mean of the prediction afterwards (as we do in the example on page 713).

Sorry if these two questions were covered in the book and I'm missing them.
You're welcome, these are good questions. Plus the book is big, so it would be easy to miss something I am afraid ...

If you could point me in the right direction for either of these, I would greatly appreciate it. Really, I should probably have included you on my committee so I wouldn't have to feel guilty asking for help!

Hope all is well.

Cheers,

-
Tyler Hallman, M.S.
Ph.D. Student
The Robinson Lab
Department of Fisheries and Wildlife
Oregon State University Corvallis

>
> I attended a workshop from you and Andy at Patuxent a couple years ago. At the time this type of hierarchical statistics was completely new to me. I've been teaching myself ever since. I bought your book (Applied Hierachical Modeling in Ecology)  MK: excellent ! ;)  , and have gone through most of the pertinent sections. I'm at the point of analyzing data for my dissertation, and I am planning on using the Time-Removal/DS model for my avian point count data. It seems like running this type of model is easier in the Bayesian framework than ML at least in part because you've shown how to do it. I don't recall seeing any way to do this type of model with unmarked in the book. Is no such function readily available in unmarked? MK: No such function in unmarked.
>
> I have one other big question, and perhaps I'm just missing this somewhere. When using unmarked, the function predict can be quite useful to predict abundance on a landscape based on a model created with unmarked. Is there a good way to make similar landscape level predictions with Bayesian models? I don't recall any examples of this in the book.
> MK: That's a quite good point actually ! I am afraid there is no direct example of this, except  for the example for species richness  on page 713.
>
> Basically, you can of course do such predictions fairly easily in BUGS software and you can do this in one of two ways:
> (1) the simplest is to provide the covariate values for all pixels in your real landscape as data for BUGS and then add a line in the code that computes the expected abundance for those sites, using (a) the parameter values estimated in the model and (b) the landscape values of the covariates provided in the data bundle. If your landscape is not too large (e.g., has less than a couple of thousands pixels), then I would probably do that. Here, of course, you will automatically get the whole posterior distribution of the predictions, so you can easily plot the predictions (meaning, their posterior mean) as well as the posterior standard deviation or the lower and upper bound of the 95% credible interval.
> (2) Especially if you have a large domain (MANY pixels), it is easier to do these predictions outside of BUGS, in R, as we do in the species richness example in the book mentioned above. Then, you take the parameter estimates from BUGS and "combine" them with the values of the covariates in your landscape to obtain the predicted abundance. In this approach it is perhaps easier to get the posterior mean only, but it is safer to obtain the full posterior of the predictions and then get the posterior mean of the prediction afterwards (as we do in the example on page 713).
>
> Sorry if these two questions were covered in the book and I'm missing them.

>
> If you could point me in the right direction for either of these, I would greatly appreciate it. Really, I should probably have included you on my committee so I wouldn't have to feel guilty asking for help!
>
> Hope all is well.
>
> Cheers,
>

Hello all,

I'm conducting multi-species occupancy models with covariates. Still figuring out how to include time effect (but that's part of another discussion).
Now I'm evaluating alternatives to conduct GoF and model selection under a Bayesian framework... always falling into this trap!

GoF: I understand Bayesian p-value is uninformative with a binary response (z in occupancy models)... so I assume I have to discard that one. There are several examples in AHM1 for N... but not for Z. Any other alternatives?

Model Selection: Using Kuo Mallick indicator variable method seems to have several complications, and not sure how to approach them. I feel AHM1 is clear about it, but it gets rough for me to code the suggested joint priors to alleviate computational problems caused by independent priors (no coding example in the book).

Any suggestions, thoughts, or code example for non-expert programmers?

​Thanks!

Andrea​

messages.body_plain:
Hello all

I apologize for taking so long to get back to the group. Life happened!

The following example could be used to provide some context. Its rather long and only really interested readers will have a look at the code.

Suppose one has compositional data. i.e. proportions taken at various times. The proportions could represent the chemical make up of different soil samples. Since one has proportions to obvious thing to do is model these proportions using a dirichlet distribution. Assuming one has covariates associated with each of the proportions which could be used to relate the mean proportion of each group to the covariate.

If the compositional data does not contain any zeros the above problem can be done fairly easily. In my problem I have what is known as structural zeros. That means that some of the proportions has to be zero!

Example

——————

- suppose we are considering 5 chemicals (A, B, C, D, E) that makes up the composition data.

- Assume that we know that one will not get A at site 1. (this will be a structural zero)

- when taking measurements at the various sites, some of the sites might not detect some of the chemicals. e.g. B might not be detected at site 2.

The idea is to model the proportions (a matrix of compositions stored in object y) using a Dirichlet distribution. i.e. y[i, for some index vector] ~ ddirich( alpha[ for some index vector] ). I wanted to use the ‘which’ function to pick out the particular elements in y that would have none zero elements and use an R type code as y[i, which( y[i,]>0 ) ] ~ ddirich( alpha[ which( y[i,]>0 ) ] ).

The problem however is that ‘which’ does not exist in BUGS and that if it did ‘the index vector’ is required to be a contiguous vector!

I decided to solve the problem by creating additional variables in R that allows me to do what I want to do. i.e. Suppose a row in y contains 1 zero in position 3, I change all of the row entries to zero and then fill the rows using only the none-zero entries - from left to right. (i.e. see the Y matrix below)  Additional data read into BUGS are

sum - the number of none zero entries in each row of y

starts - see below

ends -  see below

U - a vector that contains the indices of all of the none-zero entries in y

A simple example that solved my query. The solution is based on the following result. Suppose y1,y2,…,yn ~ ddirich( a1, …, an) then suppose we have some yi=0, the conditional distribution of the remaining none - zero entries of y is still ddirich with the same parameters as before. i.e. suppose y1=y2=0 then y3,…, yn ~ ddirich( a3, …, an )

#In R - structural zeros example

#———————————————————————

set.seed(1)

require(igraph)

n<-100 #the sample size

C<-5 #the number of compositions

#The dirichlet data

x<-t(sample_dirichlet(n, (1:5)/15))

y<-x

#lets make some structural zeros

#and the rescale the row vector to sum to 1

#add 3 in

y[1,1]<-0

y[1,-1]<-y[1,-1]/sum(y[1,-1]) #simply rescaling the data to make the row sum to 1

y[5,3]<-0

y[5,c(1,2,3,5)]<-y[5,c(1,2,3,5)]/sum(y[5,c(1,2,3,5)])

y[100,2]<-0

y[100,c(1,3,4,5)]<-y[100,c(1,3,4,5)]/sum(y[100,c(1,3,4,5)])

#indicator matrix. 'y[i,j]>0' ==> 'u[i,j]==1'

u<-y>0

usum<-apply(u,1,sum) #indicates how many elements are none-zero in each row of u

ends<-cumsum(usum)

starts<-ends+1

starts<-starts[-length(starts)]

starts<-c(1,starts)

#U is a vector that indicates which rows of y has none zero row elements

#in general all rows should have some none-zero elements!

U<-which(u[1,]>0) #assuming u[1, ] has entries with none-zero elements

for(i in 2:n){ U<-c(U, which(u[i,]>0))}

#In winbugs if one wants to use y[i,index]~ddirich()

#the index in the lhs has to be contiguous and increasing

#so I construct a new matrix for the compositions and for rows that have zeros

#I make the data start at row one and reference the appropriate entries

#using usum

Y<-y

rows_less_C<-which(usum !=C)

for (i in 1:length(rows_less_C))

{

     Y[rows_less_C[i],]<-0

     Y[rows_less_C[i], 1:usum[ rows_less_C[i] ]]<-

          y[rows_less_C[i], U[starts[rows_less_C[i]]:ends[rows_less_C[i]]] ]

}

#———————————————————————

#The BUGS code

model1<-

"model

{

     #the prior distributions of the regression parameters

     for (iprior in 1:C){ beta[iprior]~dnorm(0, 1e-3) }

     #the log link function is used

     for (jprior in 1:C){ log(alpha[jprior])<-beta[jprior] }

     #the likelihood part

     for (i in 1:n)

     {

          Y[i, 1:usum[i] ] ~ddirch(alpha[ U[starts[i]:ends[i]] ])

     }

     #store the expected proportions

     for (i in 1:C)

     {

          expected.props[i]<-alpha[i]/sum(alpha[])

     }

}"

     #I am using the jagsUI package

     require(rjags)

     require(jagsUI)

     #inputs for the Bayesian method

     niter <- 5000

     nburn <- 1000

     nthin <- 1

     nchains <- 3

     nkeep<-(niter-nburn)*nchains

     # Input data

     Data1 <- list(Y=Y, n=n, C=C, U=U, usum=usum, starts=starts, ends=ends)

     #------------------------------------------------------------------

     # Initial values

     #------------------------------------------------------------------

     inits <- function(){ list("beta"=rnorm(5)) }

     inits1=inits(); inits2=inits(); inits3=inits()

     Inits1=list(inits1,inits2,inits3)

     #Inits1=list(inits1)

     # Parameters to be monitored

     parameters <- c("alpha","beta", "expected.props")

     Run1 <- jags(data=Data1, inits=Inits1, parameters.to.save=parameters,

                  model.file=textConnection(model1),

                  n.iter = niter, n.burnin = nburn, n.thin = nthin,

                  n.chains = nchains, DIC = FALSE, verbose=FALSE)

     #str(Run1)

#print the BUGS output

print(Run1)

#Compare the expected proportions to the BUGS outputs

print((1:5)/15)

Thank you for providing some guidance!

Hi Allan,

Thanks for the clear explanation.  It looks like you found a good solution.

NIMBLE allows one to write new distributions or functions as nimbleFunctions in R for use in BUGS code, which will then also be compiled via C++.  An example of writing zero-inflated Poisson for direct use in BUGS is on our web site: R-nimble.org/examples <http://R-nimble.org/examples>.  An example of writing a Dirichlet-multinomial (generalization of beta-binomial) is on p. 41 of our user manual.

Here are two ways one could use those capabilities for your problem.

1. One could write a function that takes as input a vector of compositions and a vector of indicators of structural zeros and returns a vector with the to-be-included compositions placed contiguously, which could then be used in ddirch.  However I think that is basically what you are doing from R before going into BUGS/JAGS, which makes sense.

2. One could write a version of Dirichlet or Dirichlet-multinomial that also takes as input the vector of indicators of structural zeros and calculates the density using only the to-be-included dimensions.  E.g. one might call it dDirichletIndicator and then use that in place of ddirch in BUGS code.

I note that in a case where some of the zeros are not necessarily known a priori to be structural zeros, the Dirichlet-multinomial can be helpful.

Best wishes
Perry
